items.html: Level of measurement. It determines what can legitimately be said about two values: nominal categories can only be counted, ordinal values can be ranked, and only interval data supports statements about how much two values differ.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 48

src.question: Why does the level of measurement matter in medical research?
src.key: It determines what can legitimately be said about two values
src.explanation: nominal categories can only be counted, ordinal values can be ranked, and only interval data supports statements about how much two values differ.

items.html: Reliability without validity. A measurement can be reliable without being valid, because it can be consistently wrong. Low validity with high reliability is the combination to watch for, since repeated agreement looks like confirmation.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 59

src.question: Can a measurement be reliable without being valid?
src.key: Yes, it can be consistently wrong
src.explanation: and that combination of low validity with high reliability is the one to watch for, since repeated agreement looks like confirmation.

items.html: Construct validity. A measure has construct validity when it relates to others believed part of the same phenomenon, as in whether a clinician interviewing a patient for depression reaches the same determination as a screening test.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 53

src.question: What is construct validity?
src.key: The measure relates to others believed part of the same phenomenon
src.explanation: as in whether a clinician interviewing a patient for depression reaches the same determination as a screening test does.

items.html: Meaning of sensitivity values. A sensitivity of 0.5 means an equal chance of identifying a diseased patient. A value of one identifies every patient with the disease, and a value of zero identifies none of them.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 12

src.question: What does a sensitivity of 0.5 mean?
src.key: An equal chance of identifying a diseased patient
src.explanation: A value of one identifies every patient with the disease, and a value of zero identifies none of them.

items.html: Positive likelihood ratio of 4. A positive result multiplies the pre-test odds of the disease by four, so the odds are four times what they were before the test; the ratio is a multiplier of the odds rather than a probability in its own right.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 30

src.question: A test has a positive likelihood ratio of 4. What does that mean?
src.key: The odds of the condition are multiplied by four
src.explanation: a likelihood ratio multiplies the odds of the condition rather than its probability, so a ratio of 4 makes the odds four times what they were before the test.

items.section_title: IO 1 — Questions to ask about a new test
items.html: Blinding in test comparison. Those conducting each test should be blinded to the other's result because one result could influence the reading of the other, a form of measurement bias.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 50

src.question: Why should those conducting each test be blinded to the other's result?
src.key: One result could influence the reading of the other
src.explanation: and it is a form of measurement bias: the test would then appear to agree with the standard partly because the reader expected it to.

items.html: Validity of a test. Validity is a test's ability to determine correctly who has the disease, measured by sensitivity and specificity. Reliability, by contrast, is getting a similar result when the test is repeated under the same conditions.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 8

src.question: What does validity mean for a test?
src.key: Its ability to determine correctly who has the disease
src.explanation: and it is measured by sensitivity and specificity. Reliability, by contrast, is getting a similar result when the test is repeated under the same conditions.

items.html: Likelihood ratio formulas. The positive ratio is sensitivity divided by one minus specificity (positive result in disease over positive result without it). The negative ratio is one minus sensitivity, divided by specificity (negative result in disease over negative result without it).
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 30
4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 31

src.question: How is the positive likelihood ratio calculated?
src.key: Sensitivity divided by one minus specificity
src.explanation: which is the probability of a positive result in disease over the probability of a positive result without it.

also.key: One minus sensitivity, divided by specificity
also.explanation: being the probability of a negative result in disease over the probability of a negative result without it.

items.section_title: IO 1 — Questions to ask about a new test
items.html: Prevalence in test studies. Predictive values will differ if prevalence differs, so a published value may not transfer to your setting; check whether a study's prevalence matches your own population.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 50

src.question: Why does it matter whether a test study's prevalence matches your own population?
src.key: Predictive values will differ if prevalence differs
src.explanation: and that is the practical consequence of predictive values depending on prevalence: a published value may not transfer to your setting.

items.html: Likelihood ratio of 0.1. As a rule of thumb, it lowers the probability of disease by about 45 percentage points, mirroring the 45 point rise given by a ratio of 10; below 0.1 counts as strong evidence to rule the disease out.
cites: Assigned reading: Likelihood Ratios

src.question: As a rule of thumb, what does a likelihood ratio of 0.1 do?
src.key: Lowers the probability by about 45 percentage points
src.explanation: mirroring the 45 point rise given by a ratio of 10, which is why below 0.1 counts as strong evidence to rule the disease out.

items.html: Disagreeing tests. When two tests disagree, consider whether they ran in parallel or serially, because the two strategies do different things to the combined sensitivity and specificity.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 45

src.question: What should be considered when two tests disagree?
src.key: Whether they ran in parallel or serially
src.explanation: because the two strategies do different things to the combined sensitivity and specificity, which changes how the disagreement should be read.

items.html: Likelihood ratio of 10. As a rule of thumb, it raises the probability of disease by about 45 percentage points; the shift is added to the pre-test probability rather than replacing it, so the starting point still matters.
cites: Assigned reading: Likelihood Ratios

src.question: As a rule of thumb, what does a likelihood ratio of 10 do to the probability of disease?
src.key: Raises it by about 45 percentage points
src.explanation: and the shift is ADDED to the pre-test probability rather than replacing it, which is why the starting point still matters.

items.html: Predictive value and prevalence. With sensitivity of 99 percent and specificity of 95 percent, positive predictive value rises from 17 to 51 percent as prevalence rises from one to five percent, so predictive value depends heavily on prevalence.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 28

src.question: With a sensitivity of 99 percent and specificity of 95 percent, positive predictive value rises from 17 to 51 percent as prevalence rises from one to five percent. What does that demonstrate?
src.key: Predictive value depends heavily on prevalence
src.explanation: and the test itself did not change: the same sensitivity and specificity produced a threefold difference in what a positive result means.

items.html: Prevalence in the 2×2 table. Prevalence is a plus c, over all four cells: everyone with the disease over everyone tested. It is also the pre-test probability in the population of interest.
cites: Assigned reading: The Classic 2 X 2 Table

src.question: How is prevalence expressed in the lettered cells?
src.key: a plus c, over all four cells
src.explanation: being everyone with the disease over everyone tested. It is also the pre-test probability in the population of interest.

items.html: Why prevalence affects predictive values. Predictive values include both diseased and healthy people: each reads across a test-result row, which mixes the two disease columns in a proportion set by how common the disease is.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 26

src.question: Why are predictive values influenced by prevalence?
src.key: They include both diseased and healthy people
src.explanation: because each reads across a test-result row, which mixes the two disease columns in a proportion set by how common the disease is.

items.html: Requirement for diagnosis. Diagnosing disease requires a reliable method of detecting its presence or absence, because the task is to identify who has the disease and who does not.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 3

src.question: What does diagnosing disease require?
src.key: A reliable method of detecting its presence or absence
src.explanation: because the task is to identify who has the disease and who does not, and that is only as good as the method used to separate them.

items.html: Serial versus parallel testing. Serial testing uses fewer tests but takes more time, so the choice comes down to how urgent the diagnosis is against how costly or risky the tests are.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 47

src.question: What is the trade-off of serial compared with parallel testing?
src.key: Fewer tests used, but more time taken
src.explanation: which is why the choice comes down to how urgent the diagnosis is against how costly or risky the tests are.

items.html: False positives at low prevalence. There are usually more false positives, because the pool of healthy people is so much larger that even a small false positive rate produces many relative to the few true cases.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 27

src.question: What happens to false positives when a disease has low prevalence?
src.key: There are usually more of them
src.explanation: because the pool of healthy people is so much larger that even a small false positive rate produces many of them relative to the few true cases.

items.section_title: IO 1 — Questions to ask about a new test
items.html: Limit on diagnosis. The diagnosis of disease is limited by how good the tests used to measure it are. Sensitivity and specificity guide test selection, while predictive values describe what a given result means.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 51

src.question: What limits the diagnosis of disease?
src.key: How good the tests used to measure it are
src.explanation: and the rest follows from it: sensitivity and specificity guide test selection, while predictive values describe what a given result means.

items.html: Assessment evidence. Assessment evidence answers which tests best identify or predict a diagnosis. It sits between descriptive evidence, which characterizes patients with a diagnosis, and treatment evidence, which asks what works against it.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 7

src.question: What question does assessment evidence answer?
src.key: Which tests best identify or predict a diagnosis
src.explanation: and it sits between descriptive evidence, which characterizes patients with a diagnosis, and treatment evidence, which asks what works against it.

items.html: Named sources of medical information. Pharmaceutical representatives appear among the named sources. Their presence is not an endorsement: the list is deliberately broad, and quality has to be judged separately by peer review and appraisal.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 15

src.question: Which of these appears among the named sources of medical information?
src.key: Pharmaceutical representatives
src.explanation: and their presence on the list is not an endorsement: the list is deliberately broad, and quality has to be judged separately by peer review and appraisal.

items.html: USPSTF Grade I. Grade I means the balance of benefits and harms cannot be determined; evidence is lacking, poor or conflicting, so if the service is offered the patient should understand that uncertainty. It does not mean the balance is unfavorable.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 13

src.question: What distinguishes a Grade I statement from a Grade D?
src.key: Grade I means the balance cannot be determined
src.explanation: and the distinction matters in practice: evidence is lacking, poor or conflicting, so if the service is offered the patient should understand that uncertainty. It does not mean the balance is unfavorable.

items.html: Quality sources of medical information. Peer review marks a quality source, with government databases a further category. Be cautious of websites, which carry no equivalent guarantee of scrutiny before publication.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 17

src.question: What marks a quality source of medical information?
src.key: Peer review, with government databases a further category
src.explanation: and the matching warning is blunt: be cautious of websites, which carry no equivalent guarantee of scrutiny before publication.

items.section_title: What study design is, and why it matters
items.html: Why study design matters. Knowing each design's strengths and limits improves evaluation of evidence. Strong design produces strong data, which produces valid and reliable results, which supports better clinical decisions.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 8

src.question: Why does understanding study design matter for evidence-based practice?
src.key: Knowing each design's strengths and limits improves evaluation of evidence
src.explanation: and the chain runs further than that: strong design produces strong data, which produces valid and reliable results, which supports better clinical decisions.

items.html: USPSTF Grades A and B. Both carry the same instruction to offer or provide the service, because both rest on a net benefit judged at least moderate. Grade C offers selectively, Grade D discourages, and Grade I calls for the clinical considerations to be read.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 12

src.question: Which two grades carry the same instruction to offer or provide the service?
src.key: A and B
src.explanation: because both rest on a net benefit judged at least moderate. Grade C offers selectively, Grade D discourages, and Grade I calls for the clinical considerations to be read.

items.html: Scale of the published literature. Volume alone does not settle clinical questions: with more than two million studies, thirty thousand journals and over nineteen million citations, the answers are still incomplete.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 16

src.question: What does the scale of the published literature imply for the clinician?
src.key: Volume alone does not settle clinical questions
src.explanation: more than two million studies, thirty thousand journals, a quarter of a million controlled trials of therapy and over nineteen million citations, and the answers are still incomplete.

items.html: Breadth of information sources. Information reaches clinicians from many channels of unequal quality, running from original research journals and evidence-based databases through experts and guidelines to newsletters, representatives, media and patients.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 15

src.question: What does the breadth of the list of information sources imply?
src.key: Information reaches clinicians from many channels of unequal quality
src.explanation: it runs from original research journals and evidence-based databases through experts and guidelines to newsletters, representatives, media and patients.

items.section_title: The ABCD method for web resources
items.html: ABCD method, A. In the ABCD method for appraising a website, A stands for author, including credentials and expertise. The other three are bias, content (level of detail) and date (whether the material is still current).
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 18

src.question: In the ABCD method for appraising a website, what does A stand for?
src.key: Author, including credentials and expertise
src.explanation: and the other three follow: bias, content in the sense of level of detail, and date, meaning whether the material is still current.

items.section_title: The ABCD method for web resources
items.html: ABCD method, B. B asks about bias. It sits between the author's credentials and the level of detail in the content, so the method moves from who wrote it to why, then to what and when.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 18

src.question: What does the B of the ABCD method ask about?
src.key: Bias
src.explanation: and it sits between the author's credentials and the level of detail in the content, so the method moves from who wrote it to why, then to what and when.

items.section_title: The ABCD method for web resources
items.html: Retracted vaccine study. Publication in a respected journal does not guarantee integrity: the study appeared in a major journal and was eventually retracted, so appraisal of the author, the interests behind the work and the methods still matters.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19

src.question: What is the general lesson of the retracted vaccine study?
src.key: Publication in a respected journal does not guarantee integrity
src.explanation: It appeared in a major journal and was eventually retracted, which is why appraisal of the author, the interests behind the work and the methods still matters.

items.section_title: Clinical studies pyramid — bottom to top
items.html: Critically appraised individual articles. Also called article synopses, they sit above randomized trials because the appraisal has already been done, and below critically appraised topics and systematic reviews.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 10

src.question: Where do critically appraised individual articles sit relative to randomized trials?
src.key: Above them
src.explanation: because the appraisal has already been done. They are also called article synopses, and sit below critically appraised topics and systematic reviews.

items.html: Meta-analysis versus systematic review. A meta-analysis combines the data rather than only appraising the studies: the review identifies and evaluates the studies, and the meta-analysis statistically pools their data, so the combination works like one larger study with more power.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 14

src.question: What distinguishes a meta-analysis from a systematic review?
src.key: It combines the data rather than only appraising the studies
src.explanation: the review identifies and evaluates the studies, and the meta-analysis statistically pools their data, which gives the combined result more power than any one study.

items.section_title: Joint decision making and the five steps
items.html: Validity step of evidence-based practice. This step assesses whether the research is true. It comes before application, because research whose truth has not been established should not be carried into a patient encounter.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29

src.question: What does the validity step of evidence-based practice assess?
src.key: Whether the research is true
src.explanation: and it comes before application rather than after: research whose truth has not been established should not be carried into a patient encounter.

items.html: Judging good information. A clinician judges information by critically analyzing it and distinguishing strong from weak. A trusting patient-provider relationship and the quality of the source material behind the provider's knowledge also bear on it.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19

src.question: How should a clinician judge whether they have good information?
src.key: By critically analyzing it and distinguishing strong from weak
src.explanation: and two other things bear on it: a trusting patient-provider relationship, and the quality of the source material behind the provider's own knowledge.

items.html: Disease registry. Registries are usually established by state government to collect disease-specific data; because collection continues, they provide information about trends over time, showing how a disease behaves across years.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 16

src.question: What is the particular value of a disease registry?
src.key: It provides information about trends over time
src.explanation: Registries are usually established by state government to collect disease-specific data, and because collection continues, they show how a disease behaves across years rather than at one moment.

items.html: Good medical decision making. It depends on good information from history, examination and knowledge, and also relies on patient goals and values, provider beliefs, and the risks, benefits, effectiveness, adverse reactions and cost of any intervention.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 18

src.question: On what does good medical decision making depend?
src.key: Good information, from history, examination and knowledge
src.explanation: and it also relies on patient goals and values, provider beliefs, and the risks, benefits, effectiveness, adverse reactions and cost of any intervention.

items.html: Diagnosis question. It asks how accurate the tests used to identify the disease are, so test properties are studied as a topic in their own right rather than assumed.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 22

src.question: Which clinical question does the term Diagnosis address?
src.key: How accurate are the tests used to identify the disease?
src.explanation: The question is about the performance of the tests themselves, which is why test properties are studied as a topic in their own right rather than assumed.

items.html: Abnormality question. It asks whether the patient is sick or well, and sits alongside Frequency, which asks how often a disease occurs, as a question to settle before any answer about a patient is possible.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 22

src.question: Which clinical question does the term Abnormality address?
src.key: Is the patient sick or well?
src.explanation: and it sits alongside Frequency, which asks how often a disease occurs, as one of the questions that has to be settled before any answer about this patient is possible.

items.html: Prevention questions. Two questions fall under it: whether prevention stops disease arising, and whether early detection helps. They are different claims, since stopping disease from arising is not the same as finding it sooner once it has.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 23

src.question: Which two questions fall under Prevention?
src.key: Does prevention stop disease arising, and does early detection help?
src.explanation: and the pairing matters because the two are different claims: stopping disease from arising is not the same as finding it sooner once it has.

items.html: Sources of clinical answers. Answers to clinical questions are drawn from experience, knowledge and clinical research. Leaning on experience alone is the eminence-based reasoning that evidence-based practice was formulated against.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 24

src.question: From what three sources are answers to clinical questions drawn?
src.key: Experience, knowledge and clinical research
src.explanation: and the three are complementary: leaning on experience alone is the eminence-based reasoning that evidence-based practice was formulated against.

items.html: Practice guidelines. They are produced at the level of the hospital or clinic, nationally, and by professional bodies, such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (national) and the American Academy of Pediatrics (professional).
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30

src.question: At which levels are practice guidelines produced?
src.key: Hospital or clinic, national, and professional bodies
src.explanation: with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention among the national sources and bodies such as the American Academy of Pediatrics among the professional organizations.

items.html: Prevalence in reasoning. Prevalence prioritizes the differential diagnosis (think horses, not zebras). It also affects the interpretation of test results, because it sets the pretest probability.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 16

src.question: How does prevalence help in clinical reasoning?
src.key: It prioritizes the differential diagnosis
src.explanation: think horses, not zebras. It also affects the interpretation of test results, because it sets the pretest probability.

items.html: Cumulative incidence versus incidence density. Cumulative incidence uses a group of fixed size, whereas incidence density measures new cases in a changing population, so its denominator is person-time rather than people.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 17

src.question: What distinguishes cumulative incidence from incidence density?
src.key: Cumulative incidence uses a group of fixed size
src.explanation: whereas incidence density measures new cases in a changing population, which is why its denominator is person-time rather than people.

items.html: Narrowing the study population. Doing so may curtail generalizability. The trade is often worth making, as when a study is limited to those in a service region who need the service, but the limit has to be acknowledged.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 28

src.question: What is the cost of narrowing the population under study?
src.key: It may curtail generalisability
src.explanation: and the trade is often worth making, as when a study is limited to those in a service region who need the service, but the limit has to be acknowledged.

items.html: Surveillance and etiology. Case-control or cohort studies allow surveillance to support hypothesis testing for etiology: the data identify a question that a comparative design is then built to answer.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 36

src.question: Which study designs allow surveillance to support hypothesis testing for etiology?
src.key: Case-control or cohort studies
src.explanation: and this is where surveillance hands over to analytic epidemiology: the data identify a question that a comparative design is then built to answer.

items.section_title: Distribution of disease — person, place, time
items.html: Distribution by person. It involves profiling those affected, including behavior as well as demographics: where they eat, where they shop, what products they use, their drinking water, and whether they attended the same event.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 31

src.question: What does distribution by person involve?
src.key: Profiling those affected, including behavior as well as demographics
src.explanation: and the questions are deliberately practical: where they eat, where they shop, what products they use, their drinking water, and whether they attended the same event.

items.html: Population at risk. Only those susceptible to the disease or outcome are included; for example, men are not included in the denominator of a study of ovarian cancer.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 28

src.question: Who should be included in the population at risk?
src.key: Only those susceptible to the disease or outcome
src.explanation: and the example is unambiguous: men are not included in the denominator of a study of ovarian cancer.

items.html: Prevalence studies. They are good for generating hypotheses and planning services but poor for showing cause and effect. They are also relatively inexpensive.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 23

src.question: What are prevalence studies good and bad at?
src.key: Good for hypotheses and service planning, poor for cause and effect
src.explanation: and they are relatively inexpensive, which is part of why they are a sensible first look at what is common in a community.

items.html: Age-adjusted death rate. It is the right measure for comparing a county with its state because it removes differences in age structure; on the crude rate alone, a county with an older population would appear less healthy.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 13

src.question: Why is the age-adjusted death rate the right measure for comparing a county with its state?
src.key: It removes differences in age structure between the two
src.explanation: and without it a county with an older population would appear less healthy on the crude rate for that reason alone.

items.html: Confirming an epidemic exists. An apparent rise may reflect detection rather than occurrence, so a baseline and a settled case definition come first: both awareness and definition change how many cases are found.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 38

src.question: Why must an investigation confirm that an epidemic truly exists?
src.key: An apparent rise may reflect detection rather than occurrence
src.explanation: which is why a baseline and a settled case definition come first: both awareness and definition change how many cases are found.

items.html: Surveillance baseline. Without a baseline, a rise in cases cannot be recognized. Establishing it is among surveillance's core purposes, alongside determining the magnitude of a health problem.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 34

src.question: Why does surveillance need to establish a baseline?
src.key: Without it a rise in cases cannot be recognized
src.explanation: and establishing that baseline is listed among its core purposes, alongside determining the magnitude of a health problem.

items.html: Case definition. Most clinical information lies on a continuum, not in two boxes, so where the line is drawn between case and non-case has a marked effect on how much disease the measurement finds.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 27

src.question: Why does the case definition matter so much to measured frequency?
src.key: Most clinical information lies on a continuum, not in two boxes
src.explanation: so where the line is drawn between case and non-case has a marked effect on how much disease the measurement finds.

items.html: Cross-sectional ecologic study. It uses population rather than individual level data, relating the frequency of a characteristic to an outcome of interest across populations rather than within individuals.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 18

src.question: What distinguishes a cross-sectional ecologic study?
src.key: It uses population rather than individual level data
src.explanation: relating the frequency of a characteristic to an outcome of interest across populations rather than within individuals.

items.html: Blinding in randomized controlled trials. Single or double blinding is possible. It protects against performance bias, because participants who know they are on placebo may seek other treatment.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30

src.question: What kinds of blinding are possible in a randomized controlled trial?
src.key: Single or double blinding
src.explanation: and blinding matters because it protects against performance bias: participants who know they are on placebo may seek other treatment.

items.html: Withdrawals and drop-outs. A randomized trial must account for them because losing participants can distort the outcome. The same concern requires complete follow-up of a cohort, since participants who leave may differ from those who stay.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30

src.question: Why must a randomized trial account for withdrawals and drop-outs?
src.key: Losing participants can distort the outcome
src.explanation: and it is the same concern that requires complete follow-up of a cohort: participants who leave may differ from those who stay.

items.section_title: Randomized controlled trial — experimental, for testing hypotheses
items.html: Applicability of trial results. Results must be applicable to a larger population because a finding confined to the sample cannot guide practice. This is external validity; adequate sample size and a clear protocol are listed alongside it.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30

src.question: Why must the results of a randomized trial be applicable to a larger population?
src.key: A finding confined to the sample cannot guide practice
src.explanation: and it is external validity by another name, which is why adequate sample size and a clear protocol are listed alongside it as requirements.

items.section_title: The goal of epidemiologic and clinical research
items.html: Temporal sequence. A cohort study, starting from exposure, establishes it most directly because the exposure is recorded before the outcome occurs. A cross-sectional design measuring both at once cannot do this.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 13

src.question: Which design can establish temporal sequence most directly?
src.key: A cohort study, starting from exposure
src.explanation: because the exposure is recorded before the outcome occurs, which a cross-sectional design measuring both at once cannot do. It then waits for the outcome to appear.

items.section_title: What study design is, and why it matters
items.html: Why study design matters. Knowing each design's strengths and limits improves the evaluation of evidence, which makes the resulting clinical decision more informed.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 7

src.question: Why does understanding study design help clinical decision making?
src.key: Knowing each design's strengths and limits
src.explanation: and better evaluation of evidence is what makes the resulting clinical decision more informed rather than merely better referenced. It is what improves the evaluation of evidence.

items.html: Retrospective cohort study. The investigator identifies a past cohort, exposures are determined at that historical point, and the group is followed forward to the present to determine outcome. It is also called a historical cohort study.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 28

src.question: How does a retrospective cohort study work?
src.key: The investigator identifies a past cohort and follows it to the present
src.explanation: exposures are determined at that historical point, and the group is followed forward from there to now to determine outcome. It is also called a historical cohort study.

items.section_title: Randomized controlled trial — experimental, for testing hypotheses
items.html: Requirements of a randomized controlled trial. It needs a clear hypothesis, a protocol and random assignment, plus adequate sample size, results applicable to a larger population, and an accounting for withdrawals and drop-outs.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30

src.question: What features are required of a randomized controlled trial?
src.key: A clear hypothesis, a protocol, and random assignment
src.explanation: together with an adequate sample size, results applicable to a larger population, and an accounting for withdrawals and drop-outs.

items.html: Content validity. The measure covers all relevant dimensions and excludes irrelevant ones.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 53

src.question: What is content validity?
src.key: The measure covers all relevant dimensions and excludes irrelevant ones
src.explanation: and the exclusion half matters as much as the inclusion: a depression scale that also captured unrelated distress would fail on the same criterion.

items.html: Continuous versus discrete data. Continuous data can take any value in a range, though limited by the precision of the measurement; discrete data takes only specific values such as a number of children.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 51

src.question: What distinguishes continuous from discrete data?
src.key: Continuous can take any value in a range
src.explanation: though limited by the precision of the measurement, whereas discrete data takes only specific values such as a number of children.

items.html: Intraobserver variation. One observer interprets the same thing differently twice, such as a radiologist reviewing the same radiograph at two different times and reaching different interpretations.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 60

src.question: What is intraobserver variation?
src.key: One observer interpreting the same thing differently twice
src.explanation: with a radiologist reviewing the same radiograph at two different times and reaching different interpretations as the example.

items.html: Mean. The sum of all values divided by the number of observations; it is the best estimate of central tendency, though extreme outliers can pull it away from the bulk of the data.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 71

src.question: What is the mean?
src.key: The sum of all values divided by the number of observations
src.explanation: and it is described as the best estimate of central tendency, with the caveat that extreme outliers can pull it away from the bulk of the data.

items.html: Systematic variation. Known conditions of measurement affect the values obtained, for example blood pressure varying by time of day, after a cigarette, by patient position, or through the white coat phenomenon.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 64

src.question: What defines systematic variation in clinical measurement?
src.key: Known conditions of measurement affect the values obtained
src.explanation: with blood pressure varying by time of day, after a cigarette, by patient position, or through the white coat phenomenon.

items.html: Sickle cell trait carrier. An abnormal finding can exist without the person being sick; the converse is that a normal test does not necessarily rule disease out.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 75

src.question: What does the example of a sickle cell trait carrier illustrate?
src.key: An abnormal finding can exist without the person being sick
src.explanation: which is one half of a pair: the other is that a normal test does not necessarily rule disease out.

items.html: Ordinal values. Two ordinal values can be compared as more, less or equally desirable, but not by how much, because the intervals between adjacent categories are not defined or equal.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 50

src.question: What can be said about two ordinal values?
src.key: Whether one is more, less or equally desirable
src.explanation: and what cannot be said is by how much, because the intervals between adjacent categories are not defined or equal.

items.html: Normal distribution. Also known as the Gaussian distribution or bell curve, a symmetric shape in which mean, median and mode coincide.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 73

src.question: By what other names is the normal distribution known?
src.key: The Gaussian distribution or bell curve
src.explanation: and all three names describe the same symmetric shape in which mean, median and mode coincide.

items.html: Pre-test probability. The chance of disease before the test is done, often simply the prevalence of the disease in the population the patient comes from.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 29

src.question: What is pre-test probability?
src.key: The chance of disease before the test is done
src.explanation: and it is often simply the prevalence of the disease in the population the patient comes from.

items.html: Serial testing. Used when speed matters less, or tests are risky; it follows after simpler and safer tests have proved inconclusive, and costly tests are another reason.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 47

src.question: When is serial testing used?
src.key: When speed matters less, or tests are risky
src.explanation: and it follows on after simpler and safer tests have proved inconclusive. Costly tests are another reason.

items.html: Parallel testing. How much it improves sensitivity depends on how well each test catches what the other misses: two tests that fail on the same patients add little, whereas complementary tests catch far more cases.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 46

src.question: What determines how much parallel testing improves sensitivity?
src.key: How well each catches what the other misses
src.explanation: two tests that fail on the same patients add little, whereas complementary tests between them catch far more of the cases.

items.html: Ordering a diagnostic test. Weigh risk against benefit, the test's limits, and its cost; avoid ordering tests indiscriminately and avoid repeating a test without an indication.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 6

src.question: Which considerations apply when ordering a diagnostic test?
src.key: Risk against benefit, the test's limits, and its cost
src.explanation: alongside two instructions: avoid ordering tests indiscriminately, and avoid repeating a test without an indication.

items.html: Receiver operating characteristic curve. It is used for comparing alternative tests for the same diagnosis, since it displays the whole trade-off between true and false positives rather than a single pair of values.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 21

src.question: What is the practical use of a receiver operating characteristic curve?
src.key: Comparing alternative tests for the same diagnosis
src.explanation: since it displays the whole trade-off between true and false positives rather than a single pair of values.

items.html: Positive predictive value. The probability that someone testing positive has the disease, calculated as true positives over true positives plus false positives.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 24

src.question: What is positive predictive value?
src.key: The probability that someone testing positive has the disease
src.explanation: calculated as true positives over true positives plus false positives, which reads across the test-positive row.

items.section_title: The ABCD method for web resources
items.html: Ethical breaches in a retracted study. Improperly obtained blood and unapproved invasive tests: blood was taken from children at a birthday party for payment, and autistic children underwent colonoscopy and lumbar puncture without research review board approval.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19

src.question: Which ethical breaches accompanied that retracted study?
src.key: Improperly obtained blood and unapproved invasive tests
src.explanation: blood was taken from children at a birthday party for payment, and autistic children underwent colonoscopy and lumbar puncture without research review board approval.

items.html: Medline search tutorials. Found at the National Library of Medicine and the university library; searching and finding the best evidence is named as one of the challenges of evidence-based practice.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 24

src.question: Where are tutorials for constructing Medline searches found?
src.key: The National Library of Medicine and the university library
src.explanation: and their existence reflects a real difficulty: searching and finding the best evidence is named as one of the challenges of evidence-based practice.

items.html: Pooling data across studies. A greater number of participants usually means greater power, but pooling poor studies produces a larger poor study rather than a reliable answer.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 14

src.question: Why does pooling data across studies usually help?
src.key: A greater number of participants usually means greater power
src.explanation: and the qualifier usually is deliberate: pooling poor studies produces a larger poor study rather than a reliable answer.

items.html: Evidence-based practice. Beyond expertise and external evidence, it also considers the individual patient's situation and preferences.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 27

src.question: Beyond expertise and external evidence, what else does evidence-based practice consider?
src.key: The individual patient's situation and preferences
src.explanation: which is why evidence alone is not enough: the same evidence can support different decisions for two patients who value the outcomes differently.

items.html: Challenges to evidence-based medicine. Searching takes time, and evidence may be absent or conflicting; outdated evidence is another, and findings are often presented in language clinicians may have difficulty understanding.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 6

src.question: Which are named as challenges to implementing evidence-based medicine?
src.key: Searching takes time, and evidence may be absent or conflicting
src.explanation: and a fifth is about communication rather than the evidence itself: findings are often presented in language clinicians may have difficulty understanding. Outdated evidence is a fourth.

items.html: Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance Survey. A telephone survey of health-related risk behaviors that also captures chronic health conditions among United States residents and preventive service use.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 16

src.question: What is the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance Survey?
src.key: A telephone survey of health-related risk behaviors
src.explanation: and it also captures chronic health conditions among United States residents, which makes it a behavioral and chronic-disease instrument rather than a registration system. It covers preventive service use as well.

items.html: Publication bias. A sponsoring company may contribute because it is less likely to support research unfavorable to its product; journal editor preference is the other force keeping results that show nothing out of the literature.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 46

src.question: Why might a sponsoring company contribute to publication bias?
src.key: It is less likely to support research unfavorable to its product
src.explanation: and it sits alongside journal editor preference as the second force keeping results that show nothing out of the literature.

items.html: Population versus sample. A population is everyone in a defined setting; a sample is a subset of it.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 37

src.question: How do a population and a sample differ?
src.key: A population is everyone in a defined setting; a sample is a subset of it
src.explanation: and the definition of a population turns on the defining characteristic or setting, which is what determines whether a given sample represents it.

items.html: Confounding variable. If a placebo control group is older on average than the experimental group, age acts as a confounding variable, because it is plausibly associated with both group membership and outcome, so its effect cannot be separated from the medication's.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 43

src.question: In a medication trial, the placebo control group turns out to be older on average than the experimental group. What does this represent?
src.key: Age acting as a confounding variable
src.explanation: because age is plausibly associated with both group membership and the outcome, so its effect cannot be separated from the effect of the medication being tested.

items.html: Monitoring changes in an infectious agent. An example is resistance emerging to an antibiotic it was once susceptible to.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 36

src.question: What example is given for monitoring changes in an infectious agent?
src.key: Resistance emerging to an antibiotic it was once susceptible to
src.explanation: and it matters because the organism has not changed its name while the treatment that works against it has changed entirely.

items.html: Incidence example. In a town of 1,000 with 80 cases in 2015, 20 previously healthy people developing disease between 2016 and 2018 give an incidence of two percent; the 100 cases present in 2018 give a prevalence of ten percent.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 20

src.question: A town of 1,000 has 80 cases of a disease in 2015, and 20 previously healthy people develop it between 2016 and 2018. Which figure is the incidence for that period?
src.key: Two percent
src.explanation: since 20 new cases in 1,000 people is the new-case count over the period. The 100 cases present in 2018 give a prevalence of ten percent.

items.html: 1976 Philadelphia Legionnaires' disease outbreak. It illustrates an epidemic curve tied to a single gathering: cases were plotted by date of onset across July and August, following an American Legion convention.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 40

src.question: What does the 1976 Philadelphia Legionnaires' disease outbreak illustrate?
src.key: An epidemic curve tied to a single gathering
src.explanation: cases were plotted by date of onset across July and August, following an American Legion convention.

items.html: Surveillance. One epidemiologic function is detecting outbreaks and epidemics, alongside determining the magnitude of a problem, understanding natural history, documenting geographic spread, testing etiologic hypotheses, evaluating control strategies and monitoring changes in an agent.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 35

src.question: Which is an epidemiologic function of surveillance?
src.key: Detecting outbreaks and epidemics
src.explanation: alongside determining the magnitude of a problem, understanding natural history, documenting geographic spread, testing etiologic hypotheses, evaluating control strategies and monitoring changes in an agent.

items.section_title: Distribution of disease — person, place, time
items.html: Awareness of an epidemic. It can make new cases easier to diagnose, as with early COVID-19, so measured frequency can rise partly because clinicians started looking.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 33

src.question: What effect does awareness of an epidemic have?
src.key: It can make new cases easier to diagnose
src.explanation: with early COVID-19 as the example. It is also a reason measured frequency can rise partly because clinicians started looking.

items.html: Probability sample. Useful when subgroups such as age or ethnicity must be investigated, because a random sample of the whole population may not deliver enough of a small subgroup.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29

src.question: When is a probability sample useful?
src.key: When subgroups such as age or ethnicity must be investigated
src.explanation: because a random sample of the whole population may not deliver enough of a small subgroup to say anything about it.

items.html: Provider reporting of morbidity. It allows tracking of possible contacts and exposures.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 37

src.question: What does provider reporting of morbidity allow?
src.key: Tracking of possible contacts and exposures
src.explanation: which is what converts a report of one case into the beginning of an investigation rather than a single data point.

items.html: Starting an outbreak investigation. Determine whether the situation is epidemic or endemic, alongside the attack rate, the diagnosis and case definition, confirming that an epidemic truly exists, and characterizing it by time, place and person.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 38

src.question: What must be determined at the start of an outbreak investigation?
src.key: Whether the situation is epidemic or endemic
src.explanation: alongside determining the attack rate, establishing the diagnosis and the case definition, confirming that an epidemic truly exists, and characterizing it by time, place and person.

items.html: Proportionate mortality. The causes must sum to one hundred percent, because each cause is expressed as a share of all deaths in the population over the period.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 8

src.question: What must the causes in a proportionate mortality analysis sum to?
src.key: One hundred percent
src.explanation: because each cause is expressed as a share of all deaths in the population over the period, so together they account for every death.

items.html: Incidence. New cases arising in previously healthy people over a specified time period; prevalence, by contrast, counts everyone who has the condition.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 17

src.question: What does incidence describe?
src.key: New cases arising in previously healthy people
src.explanation: over a specified time period. That restriction to the previously healthy is what separates it from prevalence, which counts everyone who has the condition.

items.html: Random sample. Every individual has an equal chance of selection; in a probability sample the chance of selection is known but need not be equal.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29

src.question: What defines a random sample?
src.key: Every individual has an equal chance of selection
src.explanation: which is what separates it from a probability sample, where the chance of selection is known but need not be equal.

items.section_title: The goal of epidemiologic and clinical research
items.html: Good study design. Beyond comparing groups, it allows quantifying the risk difference and determining temporal sequence, which bears on causation.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 13

src.question: What does a good design allow beyond comparing groups?
src.key: Quantifying the risk difference and determining temporal sequence
src.explanation: and temporal sequence is the one that bears on causation: knowing which came first is necessary before an exposure can be held responsible for an outcome.

items.html: Cohort versus case-control study. Cohort groups by exposure, case-control groups by outcome; the cohort looks forward from exposure to outcome, the case-control backward from outcome to exposure.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 26

src.question: What is the essential difference between a cohort and a case-control study?
src.key: Cohort groups by exposure, case-control groups by outcome
src.explanation: and the direction of enquiry follows: the cohort looks forward from exposure to outcome, the case-control backward from outcome to exposure.

items.html: Cross-sectional survey examples. Varicella titres showing what proportion of a population is immune, determining obesity in a population at a point in time, and colorectal cancer screening by fecal occult blood testing.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 17

src.question: Which is an example of a cross-sectional survey?
src.key: Varicella titres showing what proportion of a population is immune
src.explanation: alongside determining obesity in a population at a point in time and colorectal cancer screening by fecal occult blood testing.

items.html: Meta-analysis. Statistically pooling data produces what works like one larger study; a greater number of participants usually means greater power, but pooling weak studies gives a larger weak study.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 32

src.question: What does pooling data in a meta-analysis achieve?
src.key: It gives more power than any one study
src.explanation: pooling statistically combines the participants of several studies, and a greater number of participants usually means greater power, though pooling weak studies gives a larger but still weak result.

items.html: Longitudinal ecologic survey. Ongoing surveillance or repeated surveys measuring trends; it may reveal an association, such as whether lung cancer incidence rises as smoking increases among women over time.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19

src.question: What is a longitudinal ecologic survey?
src.key: Ongoing surveillance or repeated surveys measuring trends
src.explanation: and it may reveal an association, such as whether lung cancer incidence rises as smoking increases among women over time.

items.section_title: What study design is, and why it matters
items.html: Study design chain. Strong design gives strong data, which gives valid results; data gathered under a weak design cannot be rescued by careful analysis afterwards.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 7

src.question: What chain runs from study design to clinical conclusions?
src.key: Strong design gives strong data, which gives valid results
src.explanation: and the first link is the one that cannot be repaired later: data gathered under a weak design cannot be rescued by careful analysis afterwards.

items.html: Secondary research. Analysis of existing data, with meta-analyses and systematic review articles as examples; primary research uses data the investigator collected personally.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 4

src.question: What is secondary research?
src.key: Analysis of existing data
src.explanation: with meta-analyses and systematic review articles as the examples. Primary research uses data the investigator collected personally.

items.html: Low validity, high reliability. Results are tightly clustered, all away from the true value. This is the most dangerous combination, because consistency is easily mistaken for correctness when nothing is checked against a known standard.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 59

src.question: What does a measurement with low validity and high reliability look like?
src.key: Tightly clustered results, all away from the true value
src.explanation: and it is the most dangerous combination, because the consistency is easily mistaken for correctness when nothing is checked against a known standard.

items.html: Statistics on poorly designed research. Statistical analysis may give a false sense of respectability to the research, because no analysis can correct for unknown biases.
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 49

src.question: What is the difficulty with applying statistical analysis to data from poorly designed research?
src.key: It may give a false sense of respectability to the research
src.explanation: and the reason it is a trap is that no analysis can correct for unknown biases, so the statistics look rigorous while resting on data that is not.

items.html: Grab sample. Researchers take whoever they can find. It is a non-random approach, alongside the convenience sample, where availability decides who ends up in the study.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29

src.question: What is a grab sample?
src.key: Researchers take whoever they can find
src.explanation: and it sits alongside the convenience sample among the non-random approaches, where who ends up in the study is decided by availability.

items.html: Qualitative research. It is naturalistic and inductive, developing descriptions. Its data are observation, field notes and audio recordings, drawn from both researchers and participants rather than from measurement.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 5

src.question: How is qualitative research characterized?
src.key: Naturalistic and inductive, developing descriptions
src.explanation: and its data are observation, field notes and audio recordings, drawn from both researchers and participants rather than from measurement.

items.html: Defining abnormality. Be careful of labeling, because cutoffs are often arbitrary and a statistically abnormal value need not mean the patient is unwell.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 77

src.question: What caution accompanies the discussion of defining abnormality?
src.key: Be careful of labeling
src.explanation: because cutoffs are often arbitrary and a statistically abnormal value need not mean the patient is unwell.

items.html: False positive. In a 2x2 table, a false positive is when the new test is positive and the gold standard negative; a highly specific test produces few of them, so a positive on such a test rules disease in.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 16

src.question: What defines a false positive in a 2x2 table?
src.key: The new test is positive and the gold standard negative
src.explanation: and false positives are what a highly specific test produces few of, which is why a positive on such a test rules disease in.

items.section_title: Clinical studies pyramid — bottom to top
items.html: Pyramid levels below case reports. In the version of the pyramid that includes laboratory work, animal research and in vitro research sit below case reports, with in vitro research at the very bottom and ideas, editorials and opinions between animal research and case reports.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 9

src.question: Which two categories sit below case reports in the version of the pyramid that includes laboratory work?
src.key: Animal research and in vitro research
src.explanation: with in vitro research at the very bottom, and ideas, editorials and opinions sitting between animal research and case reports.

items.html: Questions for any study. A provider should ask: are the conclusions valid for the sample (internal validity), and does the sample represent my patients (external validity)?
cites: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 50

src.question: Which two questions should a provider ask when presented with a study?
src.key: Are the conclusions valid for the sample, and does the sample represent my patients?
src.explanation: and the two map onto the two kinds of validity: the first is internal validity, the second external validity, which is why both have to be asked.

items.section_title: Distribution of disease — person, place, time
items.html: Levels of disease distribution. The distribution of disease is evaluated by person, place and time, and looking for patterns across those three is a large part of what epidemiologists do.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30

src.question: On which three levels is the distribution of disease evaluated?
src.key: Person, place and time
src.explanation: and the work of looking for patterns across those three is a large part of what epidemiologists actually do.

items.html: Maternal and child health rates. The rates named as specific to maternal and child health are live birth rates and fetal, infant and maternal death rates, with neonatal and perinatal death rates alongside them; all take live births rather than population as their denominator.
cites: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 6

src.question: Which rates are named as specific to maternal and child health?
src.key: Live birth rates and fetal, infant and maternal death rates
src.explanation: with neonatal and perinatal death rates alongside them, all of which take live births rather than population as their denominator.

items.html: Randomized controlled trial design. A randomized controlled trial is experimental, for testing hypotheses, because the investigator assigns and manipulates the intervention rather than observing an exposure that arose on its own.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29

src.question: What kind of design is a randomized controlled trial?
src.key: Experimental, for testing hypotheses
src.explanation: because the investigator assigns and manipulates the intervention rather than observing an exposure that arose on its own.

items.section_title: The goal of epidemiologic and clinical research
items.html: Cross-sectional design. A cross-sectional design is for generating hypotheses; it is observational, and because risk factor and disease are measured at the same moment, it cannot establish which came first.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 16

src.question: What is a cross-sectional design for?
src.key: Generating hypotheses
src.explanation: It is observational, and because risk factor and disease are measured at the same moment, it cannot establish which came first.

items.section_title: Case-control — observational, for generating or testing hypotheses
items.html: Case-control study. A case-control study is observational and can be used for generating or testing hypotheses, unlike the cross-sectional design, which generates hypotheses only.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 21

src.question: What can a case-control study be used for?
src.key: Generating or testing hypotheses
src.explanation: which sets it apart from the cross-sectional design: that one generates hypotheses only, while a case-control study can also test them.

items.html: Probability. A probability lies between zero and one, with zero meaning the event cannot occur and one meaning it certainly will; all the probabilities of events in a sample must sum to one.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 11

src.question: Between what values must a probability lie?
src.key: Zero and one
src.explanation: with zero meaning the event cannot occur and one meaning it certainly will. All the probabilities of events in a sample must sum to one.

items.html: Likelihood ratio effect. A ratio greater than one raises the post-test probability above the pre-test value, and a ratio below one lowers it; a very low ratio, below about 0.1, virtually rules the disease out.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 35

src.question: What does a likelihood ratio greater than one do to the probability?
src.key: Raises the post-test probability
src.explanation: and a ratio below one lowers it. A very low ratio, below about 0.1, virtually rules the disease out. It rises above the pre-test value.

items.section_title: Worked example — HUGIT vs endoscopy for peptic ulcer disease
items.html: Specificity in the ulcer-testing example. 9,895 of 9,975 patients without ulcers tested negative, a specificity of 99 percent; the 80 false positives still outnumber the 20 true positives, which wrecks the positive predictive value despite this high specificity.
cites: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 19

src.question: In that same study, 9,895 of 9,975 patients without ulcers tested negative. What is the specificity?
src.key: 99 percent
src.explanation: and note that the 80 false positives outnumber the 20 true positives, which is what will wreck the positive predictive value despite this high specificity.

items.section_title: Clinical studies pyramid — bottom to top
items.html: Clinical studies pyramid order. Cohort studies sit immediately below randomized controlled trials, with case-control studies and then case series and reports below; the order rises from case reports through case-control and cohort to randomized trials.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 10

src.question: In the pyramid, which design sits immediately below randomized controlled trials?
src.key: Cohort studies
src.explanation: and case-control studies with case series and reports sit below those in turn, so the order rises from case reports through case-control and cohort to randomized trials.

items.section_title: Clinical studies pyramid — bottom to top
items.html: Filtered information. Systematic reviews and critically appraised topics are filtered, as are critically appraised individual articles, meaning someone has already appraised the primary studies. Randomized trials, cohort and case-control studies are unfiltered, appraised only by the reader.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 10

src.question: Which levels of the pyramid count as filtered information?
src.key: Systematic reviews and critically appraised topics
src.explanation: and filtered means someone has already appraised the primary studies for you. Randomized trials, cohort and case-control studies are unfiltered, appraised only by the reader. Critically appraised individual articles are filtered too.

items.section_title: Clinical studies pyramid — bottom to top

items.html: Observational designs. Cohort and case-control studies are observational because the investigator watches an exposure that occurred independently rather than allocating it; the randomized trial is the experimental example.

items.html: Analytic designs. Randomized trials, cohort and case-control studies are examples of analytic work; what unites them is comparison, each setting one group against another, which supports an inference about a population.

items.html: What a meta-analysis does. It statistically combines data from multiple studies, pooling the data and weighting each study by its precision, so the combined result has more power than any one study; a greater number of participants usually means a greater ability to detect a real effect.
cites: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 14

src.question: What does a meta-analysis do?
src.key: Statistically combines data from multiple studies

items.section_title: IO 4 — Advantages and limitations of cohort studies
items.html: Prospective cohort studies and rare diseases. A prospective cohort study is impractical for rare diseases because enrollment must far exceed the few events: many more subjects must be enrolled than experience the event of interest, and it is also expensive and slow.
cites: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 16
